messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol is a 21-year-old animator who grew up in a small apartment where violence arrived without warning. Her earliest clear memories are of arguments between her mother and her mother’s boyfriend that turned suddenly physical: a plate hurled across the kitchen, a lamp striking the wall hard enough to leave a dent, her mother flinching before the object even landed. She remembers standing in the hallway, frozen by the sharp crack of something thrown and the smell of beer and hot grease from the stove, knowing that adults were screaming and that no one was stopping it. What stayed with her was not only the fear in those moments but the sense that the person causing the harm never truly answered for it. He was still around for a long time, and Marisol had come to believe that bad things could happen right in front of her and nothing would intervene.

As she got older, the memories did not settle into the past. They came back with a vividness that felt “more real than regular memories,” as if the kitchen were opening around her again instead of being remembered. If she let herself get close to the scene, she could catch the same stale smell she associates with those nights, and that frightened her enough that she would cut the memory off before it fully formed. Even so, the fragments that did break through left a mark on how she saw herself: if a memory could overtake her that completely, she felt she must be weak, unable to handle even a minor upset. The old scenes also seemed to confirm something she had long feared—that she could not stop terrible things from happening, and that the people who did them often got away untouched.

Those reactions are woven into her current life as an animator, where she spends long hours in a shared studio editing motion sequences frame by frame. Unexpected movement in her peripheral vision can make her jolt hard in her chair, and when a coworker tosses a marker onto a desk or a stylus slips from someone’s hand, her body reacts before she can think. She becomes instantly watchful, scanning the room and tightening through her shoulders, sometimes snapping irritably if someone comes up behind her. Sounds of objects hitting surfaces, images related to domestic violence that appear in reference boards or online feeds, and anything that reminds her of the man from childhood can all set this off. In those moments she feels on guard and easily angered, as though danger is already in the room.

The same cues pull the past in with them. A thrown object at work or a related photograph online can bring back the old kitchen with an almost sensory force, including the smell she remembers from the apartment, and if someone moves suddenly nearby while she is already tense, the memory becomes even sharper. She tries not to look directly at reminders of the perpetrator and will click away from certain images immediately, but the effort to shut things down often leaves her with partial, unfinished recollections that keep circling back. The more she pushes the memory away before it is complete, the less settled it feels, and the easier it is for another sound or movement to bring it back again.

Over time she has organized her life around preventing that flood. She avoids anything that reminds her of the man who hurt her family, including media, conversations, and even visual references that resemble him. After being triggered, she often copes by restricting what she eats with rigid rules because control over food feels like the one area she can still manage. She also avoids making plans for the future. Part of this is practical in her mind: when she feels this watchful and easily set off, planning ahead seems unsafe and almost naive, as if expecting life to continue normally invites disappointment. When memories break through vividly, she becomes even more determined to narrow her world to what she can control that day.

These habits have begun to deepen the very beliefs that keep her stuck. The more she cancels plans and reduces life to immediate survival, the more convinced she becomes that she cannot handle ordinary stress and that she is fundamentally helpless when something upsetting happens. Restricting her eating gives brief relief, but it also leaves her more brittle and irritable, and on edge in the studio. Avoiding reminders of the perpetrator means she never tests whether a cue can be tolerated without danger, so her vigilance stays high. And because she keeps cutting memories short rather than letting them become whole, they retain their punch; they return vivid, sensory, and intrusive, making her feel once again that the past is stronger than she is.

Marisol sought help after a recent incident at work when a colleague, acting out a motion reference, swung an arm unexpectedly near her desk and she flinched so hard she knocked over her tablet and shouted at him. She was embarrassed and frightened by how immediate the reaction was. What worries her most is that this is becoming her life—that she will remain trapped in a state of bracing, unable to trust herself with stress, unable to imagine a future, still ruled by a person who was never held accountable. What she hopes, cautiously, is not to erase what happened but to stop feeling as though every sound, image, and sudden movement can pull her back into it.
